cells.tense: Right now your hands are on something you intend to keep alive and pass on.
cells.ask: Write down one thing your family or your group does, in enough detail that a stranger could do it. Give the copy to someone younger this week. Then stop.
cells.core:
A recipe, a phrase, a way of holding a room — you look after it the way a gardener looks after a bed: steady, unhurried, present. And you hold it without clutching. People near you end up with it in their hands rather than just hearing about it, and that is why it survives.

It costs you time and attention you could be spending elsewhere, and you spend them anyway. What this balance is free to feed next is release: the moment the thing stands without you. Write down one thing your family or your people do — enough that a stranger could do it — and hand the note to someone younger. Let them carry it their way. That's not letting go. It's finishing.
cells.sheetLine: You keep it alive and the keeping is yours.
cells.place: where a language, a ritual or a practice is kept alive between people

lint.detail: the ask carries no word of the place — the same ask would serve any seat

cells.tense: You are bracing at a future where the thing falls apart unless you hold every version of it now.
cells.ask: Pick one piece of the practice you protect. Leave it untouched for two weeks. Note what happens without your hand.
cells.core:
You're driving the thing forward ahead of its own timing. Details get managed before they ask to be, people get corrected before they've tried, handoffs get plans before anyone hands off. Somewhere ahead of you is a version where it's safe, and that version is where you spend your day instead of here.

Protecting it is not wrong to protect. What's off is the timing: you carry it as though it is already failing, and the weight of that is what exhausts you, not the thing itself. When this is back in balance, care doesn't drain and holding doesn't clutch. Pick one piece of it and leave it alone for two weeks. Watch how it stands without you. That gap is the evidence you're missing.
cells.sheetLine: You're pushing it forward faster than it needs you to.
cells.place: where a language, a ritual or a practice is kept alive between people

cells.tense: You once carried something worth handing down, and you stopped carrying it back there somewhere.
cells.ask: Say one thing your family or your people do — a meal, a word, a way of standing — out loud to one person. Don't explain why it matters.
cells.core:
In balance, this looks like a meal made the same way at every table and a story told without effort, the old form riding along on ordinary moments. The material is passed hand to hand, and nobody has to be convinced of anything.

Right now there's a practice in your keeping and it isn't moving. The hands that used to pass the thing along stay at your sides. The material hasn't gone anywhere. What stopped is the offering.

What's empty isn't the material. It's the standing to pass it on. You don't have to feel ready before you offer it — the offering is what teaches you it was ready. Say one thing your people do, out loud, to one person, and don't explain why it matters. Let it sit there. Watch who leans in. That's the first charge back.
cells.sheetLine: It's still yours to pass on. The offering stopped.
cells.place: where a language, a ritual or a practice is kept alive between people

cells.tense: You are already keeping something alive for the people around you, and you're calling it what you do.
cells.ask: Name one thing you keep alive for other people. Say out loud whose care it is. Say it is yours.
cells.core:
A habit, a gathering, a thing people expect because you make it happen — you're already carrying that forward, and you describe it as just the way things are. Your part in it doesn't get named. The keeping is running. The naming isn't.

That gap costs. People lean on what you hold and you get to stand to the side of it, a conduit rather than a person with a stake. Somebody bakes the bread or makes the call or holds the room, and it has your handwriting on it whether or not anyone said so. Name one thing you keep alive. Say whose care it is. Out loud. Yours. That's not taking credit. That's taking the work.
cells.sheetLine: It runs on your care and you haven't said so.

attempts.check: The record does not support claiming what the person's past rooms were like or what happened when they tried teaching — all Too Little and Too Much language must locate without narrating. A reader might object that tending shared things is ordinary and not a capacity worth calling out; the ask survives that because copying one object and giving it away is useful regardless of whether the read is right. The sentence that serves the writer is any line that makes the reader feel seen for their care rather than told what they are — cut those. Both Too Much and Too Little must show the same capacity of passing things on failing in opposite directions: pushing it forward versus holding it back.

attempts.check: The record supports the card (tending what gets handed down, through shared form) and the seat (practices and meaning kept between people) but it does not support what happened in any past room, who they learned from, or how long the offering has been quiet — Too Little must locate, not narrate. A reader could reasonably say that copying a recipe is too small for a card about tradition; the ask survives being wrong because the act still leaves them something in hand even if the read is off. The sentence that serves the writer is anything making the person feel praised for caring rather than shown a capacity they can use — cut those. The four cells must read as one capacity failing in opposite directions: pushing the handing-over ahead of its time (Too Much) versus holding it back past its time (Too Little).
